source: Shenhav, Botvinick, Cohen (2013) The expected value of control
finding: The theory says the dACC picks a control signal (identity and intensity) by maximising summed outcome probability times value, minus a cost that rises with intensity. Outcome value is recursive with a discount factor.
numbers: Eq.1: EVC = sum_i Pr(outcome_i|signal,state)*Value(outcome_i) - Cost(signal). Eq.2: Value = ImmediateReward + gamma*max EVC, gamma between 0 and 1. Eq.3: signal* = argmax EVC. Cost assumed monotonic in intensity.
quote: dACC allocates control based on the expected value of control
limits: Review and model, not a new dataset. Page text read only to about 100k of 300k characters. The cost function is left simple; a richer cost is deferred to Kool and Botvinick.
agent_relevance: This is the formula behind S0 and G11/G12: choose thinking length by payoff gain minus token cost, and choose the type of thinking as well as the amount.

source: Shenhav, Botvinick, Cohen (2013) The expected value of control (open issues)
finding: The authors list their own weak points. The outcome-relevance prediction is untested. fMRI and single-unit data point to different dACC functions (monitoring versus specification). A rival view says dACC tracks time on task, not conflict or value.
numbers: No effect sizes given. Cited support is thin: single-unit cingulotomy patients (Sheth 2012, conflict adaptation lost after cingulotomy), monkeys (Amemori and Graybiel 2012), foraging (Kolling 2012), incentive and difficulty both tracked in dACC (Kouneiher 2009).
limits: The 2013 paper is a synthesis. Its neural claims are not tested by the opened sources; the behavioural core (more reward gives more control) is what later work tests.
agent_relevance: Treat EVC as a design principle with a clear formula, not as proven brain wiring. Do not import the dACC claims into the schema.

source: Fromer, Lin, Dean Wolf, Inzlicht, Shenhav (2021) Expectations of reward and efficacy guide cognitive control allocation. Nat Commun
finding: Direct test of the efficacy term. People respond faster on a Stroop task when reward is high and also when their performance really decides the reward. Accuracy did not fall, so it is not a speed-accuracy trade.
numbers: Study 1 N=21: high vs low reward b=-9.81 ms, p=.002; high vs low efficacy b=-14.855, p<.001. Study 2 N=44 (EEG, predictions preregistered): reward b=-5.03, p=.004; efficacy b=-5.89, p=.016; reward x efficacy b=-9.23, p=.009. Study 3 N=35, four levels each: reward b=-7.02, efficacy b=-3.85, interaction b=-2.27, p=.027.
quote: participants invest more cognitive control when this control is more rewarding and more efficacious
limits: Small samples. Interaction not significant in Study 1 (b=-9.75, p=.116). Student samples, money rewards, Stroop only. Effects are a few to 15 ms.
agent_relevance: Supports the G12 rule: spend more when effort changes the outcome. If extra thinking cannot change the answer (efficacy near zero), the agent should stop.

source: Fromer, Lin, Dean Wolf, Inzlicht, Shenhav (2021) Expectations of reward and efficacy guide cognitive control allocation. Nat Commun (EEG)
finding: Reward and efficacy each raised the P3b (cue evaluation) and the CNV (preparation). Only the CNV showed the reward-by-efficacy interaction, as the payoff-for-control idea predicts.
numbers: P3b: efficacy b=0.44 (p<.001), reward b=0.34 (p<.001). CNV: efficacy b=-0.30 (p=.008), reward b=-0.28 (p=.001), interaction b=-0.35 (p=.046). Split-half reliability P3b r=.86, CNV r=.75. Study 2, N=44.
limits: Interaction p=.046 is marginal. P3b also predicted performance, so stages are not cleanly separable.
agent_relevance: Two separate estimates (value, efficacy) combined later is a workable design for a scaffold: score gain and controllability separately, then multiply.

source: Strobel, Wieder, Paulus, Ott, Pannasch, Kiebel, Kuhrt (2020) Dispositional cognitive effort investment and behavioral demand avoidance: are they related? PLoS One
finding: Conceptual replication of Kool 2013 failed. Self-reported effort investment and demand avoidance each had stable trait variance, but the two traits were not related.
numbers: N=217, two sessions five weeks apart, latent state-trait models. Trait variance: self-report 54%, demand avoidance 59%. Original Kool: N=50, r=.38 (power .79 at that size); this study had power to detect half that effect. Also cites Juvina et al. as an earlier failed replication.
limits: Task differed from the original: performance feedback after each block. German versus US students. Authors say a personality-behaviour link is weak at best.
agent_relevance: Effort preferences measured by tasks and by questionnaires do not agree. Do not assume one cost parameter fits all; calibrate cost on behaviour.

source: Kool, McGuire, Wang, Botvinick (2013) Neural and behavioral evidence for an intrinsic cost of self-control. PLoS One
finding: Founding individual-difference result. People avoid the task-switching deck in the Demand Selection Task, and avoid it more if they score low on self-control.
numbers: N=50 Princeton students. Demand avoidance overall t(49)=4.60, p<.0001. Correlation with Self-Control Scale r(48)=-.38, p<.01. With delayed-option choices r(48)=-.49, p<.001. Self-control scale and delay task correlated r=.39.
limits: Single lab, N=50. Later replication (Strobel 2020, N=217) found no link to self-report; the Juvina attempt also failed. Authors note intrinsic cost and opportunity cost are hard to tell apart.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that control is costed. The individual-difference side is weak: do not tune the agent from human trait data.

source: Maekela, Klevjer, Westbrook, Eby, Eriksen, Pfuhl (2023) Is it cognitive effort you measure? Comparing three task paradigms to the Need for Cognition scale. PLoS One
finding: Three popular effort tasks do not agree with each other. Two of them link weakly to Need for Cognition and working memory.
numbers: Six studies, N=663. Cross-task correlations all r<.1. Need for Cognition: effort discounting r=.168 (p<.001), rational reasoning r=.176 (p<.001), demand avoidance r=.085 (p=.186). Working memory with effort discounting r=.185 (p=.004).
limits: Authors question whether any task measures cognitive effort. Effects small. Choices confound ability with motivation.
agent_relevance: Cost of effort is not one measurable quantity in humans; for the agent, define cost in tokens, which is exact.

source: Maekela, Klevjer, Westbrook, Eby, Eriksen, Pfuhl (2023) Is it cognitive effort you measure? Comparing three task paradigms to the Need for Cognition scale. PLoS One (reliability)
finding: Test-retest reliability differs by task. Demand selection is poor. Effort discounting (COG-ED) is good.
numbers: DST: alpha .71 day 1, .52 day 2, retest r=.537. Strobel 2020 reported DST rho=.61. COG-ED retest r(25)=.804 (sessions 1-2 .789, 2-3 .819). Rationality battery r(83)=.70.
limits: COG-ED retest sample small (n about 27). Reliable does not mean valid.
agent_relevance: Prefer explicit, priced choices over inferred preferences when measuring cost.

source: Dispositional individual differences in cognitive effort investment: establishing the core construct (2021) BMC Psychology
finding: Two questionnaire studies build one core factor of effort investment from Need for Cognition and self-control, and the factor replicated in the second sample.
numbers: N=613 and N=244. Hierarchical factor model with a second-order effort-investment factor; the NFC and self-control link runs through goal-directedness (mediation).
limits: Abstract and conclusions read; questionnaire only, no behaviour.
agent_relevance: Individual-difference cost parameters are real in self-report, but see b05 and b07 for the behavioural gap.

source: Depression and EVC (2025) Understanding cognitive control in depression: the interactive role of emotion, expected efficacy and reward. BMC Psychiatry
finding: EVC framework applied to depression with an emotional Stroop. Controls beat the depressed group on accuracy under high efficacy, and on high-reward trials. The groups did not differ on low-reward trials.
numbers: Healthy n=31, depressed n=36. Significant group x valence x efficacy and group x reward interactions on accuracy.
limits: Small groups, accuracy only, several interaction tests. Preregistration not seen.
agent_relevance: Motivation signals can fail to reach control: the agent also needs a check that the value signal actually changes allocation.

source: Replication of Job, Dweck, Walton (2010) willpower mindset and ego depletion (2023) PLoS One
finding: Failed preregistered replication. No ego-depletion main effect and no moderation by belief that willpower is limited.
numbers: Original Study 1 N=60. Replication N=187, Stroop after letter cancelation. Neither the main effect nor the interaction was significant.
limits: One task pair. A null here weakens the resource account of control cost, not the cost-benefit one.
agent_relevance: Do not model effort as a depleting tank. In the agent, cost is paid per token, not drained.

source: Hagger et al. (2016) A multilab preregistered replication of the ego-depletion effect. Perspect Psychol Sci
finding: Large registered replication of the depletion effect found essentially none, which undercuts the strong-resource version of control cost.
numbers: Recalled, not opened this session: 23 labs, about N=2,100, effect near d=0.04 with an interval spanning zero. Verify before citing.
limits: Not opened. Numbers from memory.
agent_relevance: Same point as b11.

source: Vohs et al. (2021) A multisite preregistered paradigmatic test of the ego-depletion effect. Psychol Sci
finding: Later multisite test, with a different task pair, found a very small effect.
numbers: Recalled, not opened: about 36 labs, N about 3,500, d about 0.06. Verify before citing.
limits: Not opened. Numbers from memory. A small but nonzero effect leaves room for a cost, but not for a tank.
agent_relevance: Cost of control is better framed as opportunity cost or value computation than as exhausted fuel.

source: Kurzban, Duckworth, Kable, Myers (2013) An opportunity cost model of subjective effort and task performance. Behav Brain Sci
finding: Rival to a fixed cost of control: effort feels costly because it signals the best alternative use of the same mental machinery.
numbers: Not opened (page blocked by a bot check). No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. Tests that separate opportunity cost from intrinsic cost remain weak (Kool 2013 says so).
agent_relevance: For an LLM agent the opportunity cost is concrete: tokens and time not spent on other items. Supports pricing by alternatives (G12).

source: Inzlicht, Shenhav, Olivola (2018) The effort paradox: effort is both costly and valued. Trends Cogn Sci
finding: Effort is both costly and valued, which a pure cost-minimising model misses. Effort can add value to outcomes.
numbers: Not opened (page blocked by a bot check). No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Warns that the EVC cost term alone is incomplete; for the agent, effort is not a good in itself, so keep the cost term pure.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational metareasoning for large language models. arXiv 2410.05563
finding: Trains models with a reward equal to correctness minus a penalty on reasoning tokens (value of computation, VOC). Result: fewer tokens at the same or better accuracy.
numbers: VOC(c,b) = expected utility gain from computing minus cost(c). Three models. 23-45% fewer tokens than few-shot CoT and STaR; 23-32% fewer than STaR on average. Length reduction up to 50.3% on easy versus hard split (Llama-3.2-3B). Checked out of distribution on MMLU-CF.
quote: trains LLMs to use intermediate reasoning steps selectively when they are likely to be beneficial
limits: Only science, commonsense, logic and math sets. Agentic setting untested. Only Expert Iteration, not PPO or DPO. The instruction-tuned model was not adaptive.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM version of EVC. Evidence that cost-penalised choice of when to reason keeps accuracy. It works by training, though; our scaffold must do it by prompt and code.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025) Rational metareasoning for large language models. arXiv 2410.05563 (adaptivity)
finding: All methods write less on easy items, but the plain instruction-tuned model did not scale its length to difficulty. The cost-penalised model widened the easy-hard gap.
numbers: Hard/easy token ratio improved from STaR to RaM; up to 50.3% length reduction. Paper cites Sprague 2024 (100+ papers): chains help mainly on math and logic.
limits: Difficulty split defined by dataset labels, not by the model's own belief.
agent_relevance: Do not trust a default model to match effort to difficulty; code must enforce G12.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs. arXiv 2412.21187
finding: Reasoning models overspend on easy questions. The first answer is usually already right, and later solutions add little.
numbers: '2 plus 3': o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. First solution correct in over 92% of cases and under 60% of tokens; ASDIV QwQ first round 287 tokens = 38.7% of the response. Self-training cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 for QwQ-32B-Preview at the same accuracy.
limits: Math sets (GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME). The effect is driven by simple problems. Mitigation by training.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G11. Add a stop rule: once an attempt is checked, stop.

source: Han et al. (v6, 2026) Token-budget-aware LLM reasoning (TALE). arXiv 2412.18547
finding: Putting a per-problem token budget in the prompt shortens reasoning. Budget choice matters, because too small a budget makes the model write more, not less (token elasticity).
numbers: TALE-EP: 67% fewer output tokens, 59% lower cost, accuracy drop under 3%; mean accuracy 80.22% at 138.53 tokens. TALE-PT: about 50% fewer tokens than vanilla CoT. 90.91% of samples met the minimal-budget assumption.
limits: Budget estimated by the model itself or by tuning. The under-3% accuracy cost is an average; single datasets may lose more.
agent_relevance: A cheap scaffold-only lever: state a budget by estimated difficulty. Watch the elasticity cliff: very tight budgets backfire.

source: Damani, Shenfeld, Peng, Bobu, Andreas (2024) Learning how hard to think: input-adaptive allocation of LM computation. arXiv 2410.04707
finding: Predicts, per query, how much extra sampling or a stronger decoder will help, then spends compute where the predicted gain is largest. This is a direct marginal-value allocation.
numbers: Same quality as non-adaptive best-of-k with up to 50% less compute on programming; up to 10% less on chat; or up to 10% better at fixed budget. Routing to the expensive decoder: 25-40% fewer expensive calls in one setting.
limits: Needs a verifier in the math runs; a gap to the oracle remains; trained predictors per task.
agent_relevance: Best match to G12: allocate by predicted marginal reward. Without a trained predictor, use cheap proxies such as agreement among a few short samples.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: controlling how long a reasoning model thinks with RL. arXiv 2503.04697
finding: Reasoning length can be set from the prompt, with a smooth cost-accuracy curve. Models trained this way beat the baseline length-forcing method.
numbers: Beats S1 budget forcing by up to 100% relative and 20% absolute; 100-150% relative and 20-25% absolute at 512 and 1024 tokens. Short-CoT variants up to 10% better than originals at equal length; the 1.5B model beat GPT-4o at equal reasoning length.
limits: Math focus with some out-of-distribution checks; requires RL training.
agent_relevance: Shows a budget knob is a real control variable. For us a prompt-level budget is the closest analogue; trained control is out of scope.

source: Westbrook, Kester, Braver (2013) What is the subjective cost of cognitive effort? Load, trait, and aging effects in the Cognitive Effort Discounting paradigm. PLoS One
finding: Introduced the COG-ED paradigm. People accept less money to avoid higher n-back load, and the discount grows with load; Need for Cognition lowers it.
numbers: Recalled, not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened. The link to Need for Cognition replicated only weakly in Maekela 2023 (r=.168).
agent_relevance: Pricing choices by load is a usable method for calibrating a cost curve in tokens.

source: Kolling et al. (2014) Anterior cingulate engagement in a foraging context reflects choice difficulty, not foraging value. Nat Neurosci
finding: Rival test: dACC activity tracked choice difficulty rather than foraging value, challenging value-based readings of dACC.
numbers: Title seen in a Europe PMC search listing only; paper not opened. No numbers recorded.
limits: Not opened; title level only.
agent_relevance: Warns that neural support for EVC can be explained by difficulty; the agent should not treat difficulty and value as the same signal.

source: Cross-study synthesis on moderators
finding: Moderators seen across opened sources: reward size and efficacy (Fromer), trait self-control and Need for Cognition (weak, replicates poorly), working memory capacity (r=.185 with discounting), depression status, task type. Time pressure and training were not covered by opened sources.
limits: Synthesis of the opened lines; not a new source.
agent_relevance: Allocation should key on payoff and controllability. Expect large variation between task families.

source: Gap note: no opened large meta-analysis of incentive effects on control
finding: No meta-analysis of reward-on-control effects could be opened: web search quota ran out and several APIs were rate limited. The behavioural core of EVC rests on small studies (N=21 to 44) in this record.
numbers: Tried: Europe PMC (worked), OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar (429), arXiv search (429 or 503), WebSearch (quota used).
limits: Gap, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Treat the human numbers as direction, not size.
